fields.expected: Most of what I've built lately is about the gap between an AI system producing an output and that output being trustworthy enough to act on. At Intelehealth I designed an evaluation framework for AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard, using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes rather than a single aggregate score. That work convinced me generation is the cheap part and judgment is the hard part. I then built a Playwright-based job-application agent where I deliberately chose determinism over autonomy: every application moves through an explicit state machine, SQLite is the single source of truth because browser automation gets dangerous when state diverges across processes, mutating capabilities sit behind fail-closed flags, and free-text and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled. Sierra is the rare place where that thinking is the actual job. Agents deployed for SoftBank, Uber, or Sutter Health talk to real customers, so failure modes are not hypothetical and craftsmanship is not a slogan. I want to work on agents with concrete users and testable failures, and I'd rather do that in person with a team obsessed with whether the thing actually works.

fields.expected: I think a great agent engineer is defined less by how much autonomy they can get an agent to take on and more by how carefully they draw the line between machine action and human judgment, and how honestly they validate what actually works. Those two things show up most clearly in the job-application agent I built in TypeScript with Playwright. Fully autonomous browser agents are dangerous in that workflow because one wrong click submits a real application or fabricates an answer, so I built it as a deterministic, operator-controlled system: every application moves through an explicit state machine, every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED that never default on, and free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled and always generate a human-review item. I also built a validation ladder from unit-confirmed through live-mutation-confirmed, because a capability passing against a local fixture is not the same as working against reality. Workday and iCIMS are detected and skipped rather than handled unreliably. Combined with the LLM evaluation work I did at Intelehealth against a 4,169-case clinical standard, that is the instinct I would bring to agents that talk to real customers.

fields.expected:
Two things that don't fit neatly into the other answers. First, I care a lot about whether things actually get used, not just whether they work. With ClarityAtlas, the iOS health app I built end to end in Swift and SwiftUI, the hardest parts weren't technical. Recruiting users into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ people, explaining repeatedly why the product should exist, and talking to institutional stakeholders mattered as much as the passive sleep-estimation system I built on HealthKit and Core Motion signals. Earlier, with SnapSort, I learned the same lesson the harder way: a technically functional system and a product people use are different things.

Second, I'm an undergraduate, class of 2029, and I'd rather be honest about that than oversell. I've built and shipped a fair amount, but the reason I want to work on agents somewhere like Sierra is to learn from people doing it at production scale with real customers.
